parts.label: Part 3
parts.article:
Hi Yasmin, shall we talk through our project on sustainable building?

Great, I've really enjoyed learning about it, especially as I didn't know much before starting the project. I was keen to know more about renewable schemes for heating and cooling buildings, and I've learned so much.

Actually, I'd always been more interested in finding out about less conventional and more sustainable materials, and also how buildings can be made to fit in with the surrounding area, which we've covered in depth. I'd learned a bit about that in my work experience last year, but I wanted to study environmentally friendly building components too, so I agree that's been really informative.

How influential do you think the regular Earth Day event has been?

Well, it's had a huge effect on attitudes to protecting the environment. The first Earth Day was in 1970, and it originated in the USA I read. The effect of environmental contamination on public health had recently been brought to people's attention in a book called Silent Spring. The Earth Day event followed on from that, and prompted changes to several laws across the globe, including some related to planning and construction. 20 years later, Earth Day went global, reaching about 140 countries, I think, and it's very influential nowadays.

Definitely. That power plant in Copenhagen in Denmark we read about was interesting.

Yes, I couldn't believe it has a ski slope on the roof and hiking trails as well. At first, I wondered what the point of it was. I suppose the multipurpose aspect is a key feature of sustainable buildings.

Right, and it's amazing what you can do there. There's a climbing wall as well. I do think it looks ugly though, such a big and noticeable construction.

Well, I think it's better than most power plants. Oh, we learned a lot from our research on that architecture firm, didn't we? I wondered if they were really as green as they said they were, but their claims turned out to be pretty accurate.

As far as we could tell, yes, it's certainly good marketing for them to add to their reputation as sustainable designers, although I think there are other firms that probably do more to promote environmentally friendly architecture.

Yes, being thought of as designing sustainable buildings must have won them plenty of contracts.

Okay, Ben, I've got a list of different buildings that we studied. And I just want to make a note of which sustainable features we were impressed by in each of them.

Good idea.

So, how about the Peace building in Malaysia? Was that the one that was entirely built with bricks that had been recovered from another building?

I think it's the one with greenery all over the walls of the building and plants to attract bees and butterflies on the roof, too, remember?

Oh, yes. It promotes biodiversity and also helps to control the temperature of the building. I love that. I remember reading about Ingel Towers.

In the Netherlands?

Yes, it's tall and slim with glass exteriors, which means it gets a lot of daylight, and that reduces energy consumption during winter.

Very clever. How about the WNT block in Mexico? We should mention that one because it has an unusual layout, which means people who live there are protected from the sun and it doesn't need air conditioning.

Yes, that's an interesting design feature. I've got the Polo on my list which is in Italy. It has solar panels and wind turbines on the roof, which keep the building running.

Right. And I think that works so well that it actually powers other local buildings as well.

Exactly. What about Simpson galleries in Zimbabwe? That uses recycled water in the heating system.

Yes, and incredibly, it's designed to still be standing in 500 years, apparently.

That is incredible. The last building on my list is One Pebble Square in the US. I want to include this one because everyone living there has the same app, which helps them to save money.

Yes, by monitoring their own heating and lighting remotely, and using the minimum necessary, really clever.

It's a great idea. OK, I think that's it, so ...

analyses.content: I think it's the one with greenery all over the walls of the building and plants to attract bees and butterflies on the roof, too, remember?
Ben 刚开始猜是“回收砖块（recovered... from another building）”建造的，但 Yasmin 纠正说是那个有植物的楼。
录音提到墙上有植物，屋顶还能吸引蜜蜂和蝴蝶，这说明建筑支持“野生生物（wildlife）”。
录音说这栋楼又高又细且有玻璃外墙，能获得大量“日光（daylight）”，对应选项中的自然光。
Yes, it's tall and slim with glass exteriors, which means it gets a lot of daylight...
虽然提到了减少能源消耗，但那是结果，设计特征是利用光照，不要过度联想其他能源选项。
We should mention that one because it has an unusual layout, which means people who live there are protected from the sun and it doesn't need air conditioning.
听到“doesn't need air conditioning”不要去选 A（雨水用于空调），因为这栋楼根本不用空调。
录音说独特的布局让住户免受日晒，不需要空调，即房间能自然保持“凉爽（cool）”。
Right. And I think that works so well that it actually powers other local buildings as well.
虽然提到了 solar panels（太阳能板），但重点不在于它有什么设备，而在于它能 power other buildings（产能过剩）。
录音提到屋顶的发电装置效果很好，不仅供自己用，还能给周围建筑供电，说明产出大于消耗。
Yes, and incredibly, it's designed to still be standing in 500 years, apparently.
录音提到了 recycled water（回收水）用于供暖，但选项 A 是回收雨水用于空调，细节不匹配，不要乱选。
录音提到这栋楼设计目标是屹立“500年”，对应选项中的“持续很长时间”。
Yes, by monitoring their own heating and lighting remotely, and using the minimum necessary, really clever.
听到 "save money" 只是结果，手段是让住户自己检查（check/monitor）能源使用。
录音说住户都有一个 APP，可以远程“监控（monitoring）”自己的供暖和照明使用情况。
